title: Draft Case Assessment Memorandum for Defective Industrial Equipment Product Liability Claim

blind.coverage: I read the instructions, all 79 criteria and all nine supplied documents in full: engagement letter, emails, damages spreadsheet, purchase order and certificate of acceptance, Ironclad standard terms, insurance declarations, OSHA citation, forensic report and incident report. I recomputed the spreadsheet's PV and total figures from its own stated inputs. Primary texts read this session: Ohio R.C. 2307.71 (definitions and (B) abrogation), 1302.98 (UCC 2-725), 1302.93 (UCC 2-719), 4167.01 (PERRP), 2125.02, and Delay v. Rosenthal Collins Group, 585 F.3d 1003 (6th Cir. 2009) via CourtListener. WebFetch was unavailable (spend limit) and osha.gov blocked curl. So these points are unverified: federal OSHA penalty maxima and Ohio's lack of a private-sector state plan (I relied only on the text of R.C. 4167.01). Also unverified: case law on OSHA-as-negligence-per-se, on the reach of choice-of-law clauses and on Ohio punitive damages (R.C. 2307.80). I did not look at the judge prompt or system prompt beyond the task description. No other Harvey LAB audits or commentary were consulted.

findings.title: Diversity criterion treats an LLC's state of organization and principal place of business as its citizenship
findings.explanation: C-063 requires the memo to 'correctly identif[y] that complete diversity exists' based on HydraCore being an 'Indiana LLC, Indiana PPB.' For diversity purposes an LLC takes the citizenship of each of its members. Its state of organization and principal place of business do not count. The record says nothing about HydraCore's members. If any member is a citizen of Delaware (Dalton's state of incorporation) or Ohio, diversity fails. A competent memo would say diversity is likely but depends on confirming the members' citizenship. That hedged answer sits between PASS ('complete diversity exists') and FAIL ('incorrectly states diversity is lacking'), and a judge may fail it. The criterion also rewards the wrong reasoning.

evidence.quote: HydraCore (Indiana LLC, Indiana PPB). FAIL if diversity jurisdiction analysis is absent or incorrectly states diversity is lacking.
HydraCore Components, LLC ("HydraCore"), an Indiana limited liability company headquartered in Evansville, Indiana

authorities.citation: Delay v. Rosenthal Collins Group, LLC, 585 F.3d 1003, 1005 (6th Cir. 2009)
authorities.proposition: A limited liability company has the citizenship of each of its members.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo analyzes diversity: Dalton is a citizen of Delaware and Ohio, Ironclad of Michigan, and HydraCore's citizenship turns on its members' citizenship. Accept either 'diversity likely exists' or 'diversity must be confirmed'. FAIL only if the analysis is absent or clearly wrong.

findings.title: UCC warranty deadline of Dec 16, 2028 uses the wrong accrual event and ignores the contract's valid one-year shortening
findings.explanation: C-066 requires a 4-year warranty deadline of December 16, 2028, 'calculated from the December 16, 2024 acceptance date.' Under UCC 2-725 (Ohio R.C. 1302.98), a warranty claim accrues on tender of delivery, not acceptance. Here delivery was November 22, 2024, with installation December 9-13. If the 24-month warranty is read as extending to future performance, accrual is instead at discovery (March 14, 2025). Section 2-725(1) also expressly lets the parties cut the period to not less than one year. Standard Terms §15.3 does exactly that for all claims, so for Dalton's warranty claims the 12-month clause is presumptively enforceable. A competent memo that treats the contractual deadline as operative for warranty claims, or dates the 4-year default from tender, would fail. Separately, §15.3's 'event giving rise' language could put warranty accrual at delivery, which makes a conservative protective date earlier than March 14, 2026 (C-035) defensible too.

evidence.quote: identifies the 4-year UCC warranty statute of limitations with a deadline of December 16, 2028 (calculated from the December 16, 2024 acceptance date)
MUST BE COMMENCED WITHIN TWELVE (12) MONTHS AFTER THE DATE ON WHICH THE CLAIM OR CAUSE OF ACTION ACCRUES
The Equipment was delivered to Buyer's facility at 4500 Industrial Parkway, Dayton, Ohio 45414 on November 22, 2024.

authorities.proposition: Four-year period; 'By the original agreement the parties may reduce the period of limitation to not less than one year'; 'A breach of warranty occurs when tender of delivery is made,' except for warranties that explicitly extend to future performance, which accrue on discovery.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo analyzes the warranty limitations period, whether by recognizing that the contractual 12-month period likely governs warranty claims under UCC 2-725(1) or by stating a 4-year default from tender or discovery (roughly late 2028 to March 2029). Drop the requirement that the period run from acceptance.

findings.title: C-036 treats the 12-month clause as binding contract claims while C-066 requires a 4-year warranty deadline
findings.explanation: C-036 rewards a memo that finds the 12-month contractual period potentially applicable to 'commercial/contract claims' and unenforceable only for tort claims. Warranty claims are contract claims. If the clause binds them, as UCC 2-725(1) permits, the operative warranty deadline is the contractual one, not December 16, 2028. C-066 nonetheless requires the 4-year date. A memo that is consistent with C-036 is pushed toward failing C-066, unless it states both dates without saying which one controls.

evidence.quote: distinguishing between its potential applicability to commercial/contract claims versus its likely unenforceability for tort claims
FAIL if this deadline is not stated or is materially incorrect.

authorities.proposition: Parties may contractually reduce the UCC limitation period to not less than one year.

findings.suggested_fix: Reframe C-066 as a conditional: the 4-year UCC period applies only if the contractual shortening is not enforced against the warranty claims.

findings.title: Dalton loss totals adopt a spreadsheet figure that leaves out the destroyed $1.29M press and the two die sets
findings.explanation: The incident report says the HX-9000 itself 'is likely a total loss' (purchase price $1,287,500) and that two custom die sets were destroyed. The spreadsheet's 'Total Dalton Direct Losses' of $1,673,750 includes neither; its only equipment item is the $189,000 Haas mill. The press is recoverable at least in warranty, since the §10.3 remedy includes a refund of the purchase price. A careful memo that corrects the total to about $2.96M falls outside C-057's 5% band. The same correction pushes the low aggregate to about $13.07M, outside C-059's 10% band (upper limit about $12.96M). A memo that reports the spreadsheet figure and separately flags the omission would pass. So this misgrades some competent answers, and it penalizes the better analysis.

evidence.quote: Catastrophic damage. The press is inoperable and is likely a total loss. Purchase price was \$1,287,500.
or a figure within 5% of $1,673,750, i.e., between $1.59M and $1.76M

findings.suggested_fix: Accept either the spreadsheet total ($1.67M) or a corrected total that adds the press and dies, if it is explained. Widen C-059 the same way.

findings.title: The $1.89M lost-earnings present value cannot be reproduced from the spreadsheet's own stated inputs
findings.explanation: The spreadsheet says the PV is based on $79,600 a year, 2.5% growth, a 3.0% discount rate and 31 years. A standard growing-annuity calculation on those inputs gives about $2.23M (about $2.28M if growth starts in year 1), not $1.89M. Using the stated assumptions, household services come to about $211K, not $195K. Also, Ohio wrongful-death economic loss is loss of support, which ordinarily nets out the decedent's personal consumption, so a gross-earnings PV overstates it. A memo that recomputes or adjusts the figure would state something other than 'approximately $1.89M' and could fail. Most memos will adopt the expert's number and pass.

evidence.quote: PV calculation: $79,600/yr, 2.5% growth, 3.0% discount, 31 years' | D19='$1,890,000'
FAIL if the lost earnings PV figure is not stated or is substantially wrong.

authorities.proposition: Wrongful death action brought by personal representative for the benefit of spouse, children and parents; damages proportioned to beneficiaries' loss.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo reports Dr. Voigt's $1.89M figure, or a recomputed or adjusted figure with its basis explained.

findings.title: Requires negligence as a separate product-liability theory although Ohio's product liability act abrogates common-law product claims
findings.explanation: R.C. 2307.71(B) states that the Ohio Products Liability Act (OPLA, R.C. 2307.71-2307.80) is 'intended to abrogate all common law product liability claims or causes of action.' Negligence-based claims for death, injury or damage to other property therefore proceed as statutory defect claims (2307.74-.77), not as a stand-alone negligence count. Negligence survives only at the margins: for pure economic loss outside the 'product liability claim' definition, for negligent installation as a service, or if Michigan law applied. A memo that correctly organizes liability under the statutory OPLA claims and never pleads 'negligence' separately fails C-009, which demands 'negligence as a separate theory.' A memo that discusses negligence and explains why it is abrogated should pass.

evidence.quote: FAIL if negligence as a separate theory of liability is not discussed.

authorities.proposition: Sections 2307.71 to 2307.80 are intended to abrogate all common law product liability claims or causes of action.
'Product liability claim' covers death, physical injury, emotional distress, or physical damage to property other than the product in question.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo discusses negligence-based liability, including under the statutory framework of R.C. 2307.71-.80, or explains its abrogation or limited survival (economic loss, negligent installation).

findings.title: Criteria rest cap unenforceability on unconscionability or public policy and misstate UCC 2-719(3)'s consumer-goods rule
findings.explanation: The personal injury and wrongful death claims belong to Reyes's estate, Trask and Anand, who never signed the contract. The main reason §12's cap and exclusion do not limit their tort claims is lack of privity; §15.8 (no third-party beneficiaries) supports this. C-016 requires the conclusion to cite 'unconscionability or public policy grounds', so a memo resting on non-party status could fail. C-017 frames the governing rule as 'consumer/defective goods' being 'prima facie unconscionable.' But R.C. 1302.93(C) limits that presumption to consumer goods and says a limitation where 'the loss is commercial is not' prima facie unconscionable. A 4,000-ton industrial press is not a consumer good. C-017 also lists OPLA (2307.72 et seq.) as authority for a proposition it does not contain. The 'or equivalent' wording softens this.

evidence.quote: citing unconscionability or public policy grounds
limitations of consequential damages for personal injury from consumer/defective goods are prima facie unconscionable
Nothing in these Terms, express or implied, is intended to or shall confer upon any third party (including without limitation any employee...

authorities.proposition: Limitation of consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable, but limitation of damages where the loss is commercial is not.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept non-signatory or privity reasoning as a ground in C-016. In C-017, state 2-719(3) accurately (consumer goods) and accept any sound authority, including privity principles.

findings.title: Measures the $11.8M-$18.8M total claim value against Dalton's CGL limit without the premise that makes the comparison meaningful
findings.explanation: The $11.8M-$18.8M figure is the sum of claims by the employees and by Dalton against Ironclad and HydraCore. Dalton is the plaintiff. Workers' compensation exclusivity largely shields it from the employees' claims, and the CGL excludes employee bodily injury, including 'any obligation of the insured to indemnify or contribute.' The spreadsheet itself notes the CGL does not cover Dalton's affirmative claims. The comparison makes sense only through an unstated route, such as Dalton's §11.1(d) duty to indemnify Ironclad for employee claims, and that route is itself excluded from coverage. A memo that correctly says the CGL and umbrella are largely beside the point for these claims may never frame a 'gap between exposure and the $5M CGL limit' and could fail C-044. C-045 is similar but easier to satisfy.

evidence.quote: Dalton is the PLAINTIFF here — CGL does not cover Dalton's affirmative claims against Ironclad/HydraCore.
or to any obligation of the insured to indemnify or contribute with another because of damages arising out of such injury
FAIL if the gap between exposure and the $5M CGL limit is not identified.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo compares aggregate claim values with available coverage, or explains why Dalton's liability policies do not respond (plaintiff posture, employer's liability exclusion, uninsured contractual indemnity exposure).

findings.title: Choice-of-law criterion presumes Michigan law covers only contract claims, but §15.1 expressly reaches all disputes
findings.explanation: Section 15.1 applies Michigan law to 'all disputes arising out of or related to' the terms, the PO, or the Products. That broad wording can reach tort claims between the contracting parties. A competent memo could conclude that Michigan law may govern Dalton's own tort and property claims but not the non-signatory employees' tort claims, which Ohio law governs. That divides the claims by party rather than by claim type. C-041 requires the conclusion that the clause governs contract claims 'but not tort claims,' so this reasonable answer may be failed.

evidence.quote: THESE TERMS AND ALL DISPUTES ARISING OUT OF OR RELATED TO THESE TERMS, ANY PURCHASE ORDER, OR THE PRODUCTS SHALL BE GOVERNED BY ... THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF MICHIGAN
concludes that it likely governs contract/warranty claims but not tort claims (strict liability, negligence), which would be governed by Ohio law

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo analyzes the clause's reach and makes any reasoned distinction, by claim type or by signatory status, rather than applying Michigan law wholesale.

findings.title: Venue criterion requires a choice between two Ohio courts and ignores the Kent County, Michigan forum clause and arbitration
findings.explanation: For Dalton's own claims, §14 requires AAA arbitration in Grand Rapids, and §15.2 names state and federal courts in Kent County, Michigan as the exclusive forum for non-arbitrable disputes. A competent memo may conclude that Dalton's contract and commercial claims are likely headed to Grand Rapids arbitration or Kent County. It may then recommend an Ohio forum only for the non-signatories' claims, or recommend resisting arbitration, without choosing between the Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas and S.D. Ohio. C-062 would fail that memo. Any state-court choice also carries a removal risk the criterion does not mention.

evidence.quote: Buyer hereby irrevocably consents to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of the state and federal courts located in Kent County, Michigan
makes a recommendation on whether to file in Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas (Ohio state court) or U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio (Dayton)

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo makes a reasoned forum recommendation that accounts for the arbitration and forum-selection clauses, whichever forum it picks.

findings.title: Coverage checklist calls ten topics 'requested' when the instructions list six
findings.explanation: The instructions ask for liability, defenses, damages, insurance, venue strategy, and an action plan. C-067 requires at least 9 of 10 topics, adding executive summary, workers' compensation interaction, representation and conflict considerations, and evidence preservation, and fails a memo if any two are 'entirely absent.' An executive summary is standard for this document type, and preservation fits naturally in an action plan. A dedicated representation or conflicts discussion is not implied by the six requested topics. A memo that follows the instructions and treats workers' compensation only as a damages offset could be failed. The title's claim that all ten were 'requested' is inaccurate.

evidence.quote: draft a case assessment memo covering liability, defenses, damages, insurance, venue strategy, and recommended action plan
Memo covers all 10 requested topics (threshold: no more than 1 absent)

findings.suggested_fix: Limit the checklist to the six requested topics plus an executive summary. Grade workers' compensation, conflicts and preservation through their own specific criteria.

findings.title: OSHA citation is issued by an Ohio agency under R.C. Chapter 4167, which covers only public employers
findings.explanation: The citation claims authority under R.C. Chapter 4167 and was issued by the 'Ohio Division of Safety & Hygiene' to a private manufacturer. Chapter 4167 is the Public Employment Risk Reduction Program, which defines covered employers as the state and political subdivisions. As I understand it (not verified this session), private employers in Ohio fall under federal OSHA, where contests go to the federal Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission (OSHRC). A careful memo could reasonably flag that the issuing authority or the contest forum is defective, and that bears on the contest strategy (C-073) and on the evidentiary weight analysis (C-029). The record also conflicts internally. The citation says the accumulator valve lacked a lockout hasp, while the forensic report says it had one. That is useful contest evidence rather than a defect. The criteria still grade correctly on the numbers, so the effect on grading is limited.

evidence.quote: Pursuant to the authority vested in the Ohio Division of Safety & Hygiene under Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4167
The single isolation valve on the accumulator circuit did not have a built-in lockout hasp
The accumulator circuit's energy-isolating device consisted of a manual ball valve equipped with a lockout hasp.

authorities.proposition: Chapter 4167 (Public Employment Risk Reduction Program) defines 'public employer' as the state, political subdivisions, and their instrumentalities.

findings.suggested_fix: Reissue the citation as a federal OSHA citation from an Ohio area office, or add a note that the scenario assumes Ohio enforcement. Accept memos that flag the jurisdictional anomaly.

blind.overall: The rubric mostly tracks the record: the party facts, forensic findings, damages figures, emails, OSHA details and insurance terms match the supplied documents. Two criteria state wrong law in a way likely to fail competent memos. C-063 treats an LLC's state of organization and principal place of business as its citizenship. C-066 dates the UCC warranty period from acceptance and ignores the contract's valid one-year shortening, which also sits uneasily with C-036. A second group inherits the spreadsheet's errors: Dalton's total omits the destroyed $1.29M press, and the $1.89M present value cannot be reproduced from its own inputs. Another group presumes a single legal route: unconscionability rather than privity for the liability cap, negligence as a stand-alone theory despite R.C. 2307.71(B), contract-versus-tort choice of law despite §15.1's broad wording, and a choice between two Ohio forums despite the arbitration and Kent County clauses. The rest are demanding checklist items rather than defects. Under the all-pass metric, the two problematic criteria alone could zero out strong answers.

sol_verdicts.reason: I re-read Delay v. Rosenthal Collins, 585 F.3d 1003, 1005 (6th Cir. 2009), which holds that an LLC has the citizenship of each of its members. The record gives only HydraCore's state of organization and its headquarters, not its members. So C-063 requires an unconditional 'complete diversity exists' on the wrong test. A correct conditional answer falls between its PASS and FAIL conditions.

R.C. 1302.93(C) (re-read) makes the prima facie unconscionability presumption apply only to consumer goods and says a limit on 'commercial' loss is not prima facie unconscionable. C-017's PASS text states the principle for 'consumer/defective goods', and this is a 4,000-ton industrial press. So the criterion states wrong law and rewards a memo that applies the consumer presumption. The real ground for the injured non-parties is lack of privity.

R.C. 1302.98(B) (re-read) says a warranty breach occurs on tender of delivery, or on discovery for a warranty of future performance. It does not run from acceptance. Delivery was Nov 22, 2024. Section 1302.98(A) also lets the parties shorten the period to one year, and §15.3 does that. So a mandatory Dec 16, 2028 deadline fails correct memos.

Section 15.1 reaches 'all disputes arising out of or related to' the Terms, the PO or the Products. A reasoned memo could apply Michigan law to Dalton's own tort claims and Ohio law to the non-signatories. That divides the claims by party, not by claim type. C-041 requires the contract/tort split, but that split remains a defensible majority view, so the criterion is arguable rather than wrong.

The document defect is real: osha.gov confirms Ohio has no OSHA-approved State Plan and is under federal jurisdiction, yet the citation comes from an Ohio agency under R.C. Ch. 4167. But C-026 and C-027 only require reciting the regulation and penalty. C-073's 15-working-day contest window matches federal practice. A memo that flags the anomaly still passes all three. I keep the defect as a finding tied to no criterion.

Dalton is the plaintiff. The spreadsheet itself says the CGL does not cover Dalton's affirmative claims, and the employer's-liability exclusion covers indemnity obligations. So comparing total claim value with the $5M CGL limit has a mistaken premise. A memo that correctly says the policies do not respond may never frame that 'gap', which is the risk for C-044. C-045's FAIL test is easier to meet, because explaining why the umbrella does not respond arguably discusses its adequacy.

An executive summary is a standard part of a case assessment memo, so it is implicit rather than hidden; C-067 lists it too. C-002 through C-005 ask for facts any competent summary of this matter would contain: the incident, the death, the injuries and Dalton's losses. These criteria are demanding checklist items, not defects.

ANSI and GlobalSpec catalog listings (search results, not the licensed text) give NFPA/T2.6.1 as a fatigue and burst-pressure rating test method (R2-2001, reaffirmed). It is not a 2020 'System and Component Safety' recommended practice. The forensic report therefore misdescribes it, and C-071 rewards repeating that description. I could not verify ISO 4413 cl. 5.4.7.2. The grading impact is low, because citing the expert's standards passes.

R.C. 2307.71(B) (re-read) abrogates 'all common law product liability claims.' A memo that organizes liability entirely under the statutory OPLA defect claims could fail C-009's 'negligence as a separate theory.' A memo that discusses negligence and explains its abrogation should pass, so the criterion is arguable, not problematic.

A memo that rests on privity with little formal authority risks failing.

Most memos will adopt the expert's figure and pass.

evidence.quote: PV calculation: $79,600/yr, 2.5% growth, 3.0% discount, 31 years
FAIL if the lost earnings PV figure is not stated or is substantially wrong.

authorities.proposition: Wrongful death damages are for the benefit of the spouse, children and parents and measured by their loss, including loss of support.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo reports Dr. Voigt's $1.89M, or a recomputed or adjusted figure with its basis explained.

findings.title: Venue criterion requires a choice between two Ohio courts and ignores the Grand Rapids arbitration and Kent County forum clauses
findings.explanation: Section 14 sends disputes to AAA arbitration in Grand Rapids, and §15.2 names the Kent County, Michigan courts as the exclusive forum otherwise. Dalton, the client, is the party bound by both clauses. A competent memo might recommend Grand Rapids arbitration or Kent County for Dalton's claims, or a strategy for resisting arbitration, without choosing between Montgomery County Common Pleas and S.D. Ohio. C-062's PASS names only those two Ohio courts, while its FAIL is only 'no venue recommendation.' That memo lands between the two.

evidence.quote: Buyer hereby irrevocably consents to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of the state and federal courts located in Kent County, Michigan
makes a recommendation on whether to file in Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas (Ohio state court) or U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio (Dayton)

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo makes a reasoned forum recommendation that accounts for the arbitration and forum-selection clauses.

findings.title: Coverage checklist calls ten topics 'requested' when the instructions list six
findings.explanation: The instructions list six topics. C-067 adds workers' compensation interaction, representation and conflicts, and evidence preservation, and fails a memo missing any two of its ten. The executive summary is implicit in the document type, and preservation fits naturally within an action plan. A dedicated conflicts section is not implied by the six requested topics. The risk is limited because workers' compensation will usually come up.

evidence.quote: draft a case assessment memo covering liability, defenses, damages, insurance, venue strategy, and recommended action plan
Memo covers all 10 requested topics (threshold: no more than 1 absent)

findings.suggested_fix: Limit the checklist to the six requested topics plus an executive summary. Grade the other topics through their specific criteria.

findings.title: Forensic report and C-071 misdescribe NFPA T2.6.1 as a 2020 system-safety practice requiring redundant pressure relief
findings.explanation: The forensic report cites 'NFPA T2.6.1-2020 (Recommended Practice — Hydraulic Fluid Power — System and Component Safety), Section 7.3.4' as requiring a secondary relief valve. Public catalog listings give NFPA/T2.6.1 as a method for verifying fatigue and establishing burst pressure ratings of fluid power components, R2-2001 and reaffirmed since. That is not a 2020 system-safety practice. C-071 rewards presenting it as calling for redundant relief. I could not verify ISO 4413:2010 clause 5.4.7.2. The grading impact is low because C-071 accepts either standard and citing the expert passes, but the criterion rests on a misdescribed standard.

evidence.quote: **NFPA T2.6.1-2020** (*Recommended Practice --- Hydraulic Fluid Power --- System and Component Safety*), Section 7.3.4, provides:
references industry standards (NFPA T2.6.1-2020 and/or ISO 4413:2010) as calling for redundant pressure relief on accumulator circuits

authorities.citation: NFPA/T2.6.1 R2-2001 (R2019), ANSI webstore catalog listing
authorities.proposition: Title: 'Fluid power components - Method for verifying the fatigue and establishing the burst pressure ratings of the pressure containing envelope of a metal fluid power component.'

findings.suggested_fix: Correct the standard citation in the forensic report, or have the criterion credit the expert's opinion as attributed rather than as a verified standard.

findings.title: Private-employer OSHA citation issued by an Ohio agency although Ohio is under federal OSHA; engagement letter predates the citation
findings.explanation: The citation is issued to a private manufacturer by the 'Ohio Division of Safety & Hygiene' under R.C. Ch. 4167, and contests and payment go to that Division. osha.gov states that Ohio has no OSHA-approved State Plan and that federal OSHA covers most private-sector workers there. Contests of federal citations go to OSHRC. Separately, the engagement letter dated March 22, 2025 refers to 'the OSHA citations issued', but the citation's issuance date is April 28, 2025. No criterion misgrades because of these points: C-026, C-027 and C-073 are met by accurate recitation, and the 15-working-day window matches federal practice. But the defects could confuse the solver about the contest forum.

evidence.quote: Pursuant to the authority vested in the Ohio Division of Safety & Hygiene under Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4167
**Issuance Date:**                  April 28, 2025
Analyzing and responding to the OSHA citations issued against Dalton (Inspection No. OH-2025-04218)

authorities.proposition: Ohio is not an OSHA-approved State Plan and is under federal OSHA jurisdiction, which covers most private sector workers within the state.

findings.suggested_fix: Reissue the citation as a federal OSHA area-office citation with an OSHRC contest procedure, and fix the dates in the engagement letter. Accept memos that flag the anomaly.

final.changes_from_blind:
1. C-017 is split out of blind O7 and upgraded to problematic (now O3). Its PASS text states the 2-719(3) presumption for 'consumer/defective goods', which I re-read R.C. 1302.93(C) to confirm is wrong, so under the task's definition it states wrong law. C-016 stays arguable (O4).
2. C-071 is adopted from Sol F8 as an arguable document defect (O12). Catalog listings show NFPA/T2.6.1 is a fatigue and burst-pressure test method, not the 2020 system-safety practice the forensic report cites.
3. Blind O12 (OSHA issuing authority) is revised into O13, a document defect tied to no criterion. On review, C-026, C-027, C-029 and C-073 are all satisfied by accurate recitation, and the 15-working-day window matches federal practice. I added the engagement-letter date anomaly and verified Ohio's federal-OSHA status on osha.gov.
4. Blind O3 (C-036 vs C-066) is folded into O2. I dropped C-036 and C-035 as defects: C-036 states correct law, and March 14, 2026 is a correct contractual date for Dalton's tort and property claims.
5. Sol F7 (C-001 to C-005, executive summary) is rejected: an executive summary is a standard part of a case assessment memo.
6. Verification: I re-read R.C. 1302.98, 1302.93, 2307.71 and Delay this session. I marked R.C. 2125.02 unverified and removed R.C. 4167.01.
final.overall: The rubric generally matches the record, but three criteria state wrong law and could zero out strong memos under all-pass. C-063 applies corporate citizenship rules to an LLC. C-066 dates the UCC warranty period from acceptance rather than tender and ignores the valid one-year contractual limit. C-017 extends 2-719(3)'s consumer-goods presumption to an industrial press. A second group is arguable. Some presume one legal route: C-016 on unconscionability, C-009 on separate negligence, C-041 on the contract/tort split and C-062 on a choice between two Ohio forums. Others inherit spreadsheet or report errors (C-057, C-059, C-060, C-071), frame coverage oddly (C-044, C-045) or broaden the requested topics (C-067). Two record defects, the Ohio-issued private OSHA citation and the misdescribed NFPA standard, are real but mostly do not change grading. Of Sol's findings, I reject F5 and F7 at the criterion level and agree with the rest.
final.coverage: In this pass I read the instructions and 17 key criteria in full. I re-checked the documents for the facts behind each disputed criterion: the OSHA citation dates, authority and penalties, the forensic report's standards citations, the damages spreadsheet, the engagement letter and the Terms §§14-15. My blind pass had covered all 79 criteria and 9 documents. Primary texts read this session: R.C. 1302.98, 1302.93 and 2307.71 on codes.ohio.gov, osha.gov/stateplans, and Delay v. Rosenthal Collins, 585 F.3d 1003, on CourtListener. The NFPA/T2.6.1 title comes from catalog listings in search results, not the licensed text, so I marked it unverified. ISO 4413 clause text, R.C. 2125.02 and the federal OSHA penalty maxima are also unverified. I read Sol's index entry and full report.
